As much as I respect Ron Paul this endorsement seems pretty shaky. Ever since getting burned by Obama I've been a lot more careful about supporting any politician. Here are a few things I discovered and considered in checking out Rand Paul:

  • Everybody knows about his 14.5% 'flat tax' idea. And I think most also realize this would be an unbelievably huge handout to the super wealthy in our country. Things like special capital gains taxes would be eliminated altogether. What most people don't realize is that it would actually be a tax increase on the majority of non-rich Americans. It being 14.5% is apparently intended to make it seem that if you earn more than $9,225 per year (which would put you in the 15% tax bracket) that it'd be a tax cut. So how can it be a tax increase for most Americans? The current median income in the US is $27,851 so 50% earn even less than that. How much tax do you pay on $27,851? Well it puts you in the 15% tax bracket, but we have a progressive taxation scheme. That means if you earn $27,851 you don't pay 15% on $27,851 but pay 10% on the first $9225 and then 15% * on the remaining $18,626. That's a total tax bill of $3716.40 or 13.3% overall. You'd see a tax increase of about 10% under Rand's flat tax. This tax plan is intentionally being spun as a tax reduction for everybody when I know Rand obviously knows it's not. That rubs me even worse than a candidate trying to raise taxes on the poor and middle class.

  • He's untested. He's only been in office since 2011. The thing I think everybody has learned from Obama is that you should only trust a politician as far as you can throw them. Record is everything. Even ostensibly going against your party doesn't mean much, particularly with primaries and elections just around the corner.

  • He's also not going anywhere near as far his father did on topics like the Federal Reserve. While Ron wanted to abolish the Fed and return to a value backed currency, Rand merely wants to 'audit' the Fed. It's already audited in fact and this would likely do nothing more than open up the door to further politicizing the monopoly money we call the greenback. But it's just enough to try to align him with his father's supporters. It reeks of politicking to me.

I'd be extremely cautious if suddenly he starts getting major air time from places like Fox. His record and actions are not entirely fitting up with his rhetoric which is something I think should be sending off alarm bells for everybody. Similarly I'd be careful about convincing yourself he's just 'playing ball' to try to get things done. It's the same game I, and I think many others, played with Obama and look at what we got. That said Obama did not have the endorsement of somebody like Ron Paul who is probably going to have a better idea of Rand's motivations than most anybody except Rand himself. But fool me once, shame on you... fool me twice, shame on me.
